title: Dependency tracking software
metaDescription: Husn tracks dependencies live across Jira, Slack, and docs and alerts the team about to be blocked when the other side moves, before the list goes stale.
heroEyebrow: For teams tracking many moving handoffs
heroHeadline: Tracking that alerts before the block.
heroSubheadline: Most tracking tools record a dependency and stop watching it. Husn keeps watching, so when one side shifts you hear about it while there is still time to act.
primaryPain: A dependency list answers the wrong question. It tells you what people intended at the moment they typed it in, not what is true today. By the time the gap shows up, the team that was waiting has already lost the time it needed to react.
painBullets: The list is accurate the day it is built and a little less accurate every day after, with no signal telling you which entries went stale.
Tracking the date is easy. Tracking whether the other side still plans to deliver on that date is the part nobody does.
When a dependency does slip, the alert comes from a frustrated person, not the tool, and it comes late.
whyHardHeading: Why tracking falls behind the work
whyHard: A dependency lives in two boards at once, and a tracker that watches one board misses every change made on the other.
The status that matters is intent, and intent changes in a Slack thread or a reprioritized ticket long before anyone updates the tracker.
Alerts based on dates fire when the date arrives, which is the moment it is already too late to do anything useful.
howHusnHelps: Husn tracks each dependency from the live work across Jira, Slack, and docs, so a paused ticket or a quiet thread updates its state automatically.
It alerts the waiting team when the other side changes intent or timing, not when the deadline lands, so the warning arrives early enough to matter.
You see the current state of every tracked dependency in one place, with the source behind each change rather than a flat list of dates.

useCases.body: See each dependency as it stands today, updated from the work, instead of a record that froze the day it was entered.

useCases.body: Get alerted when the other side goes quiet or changes course, before the date arrives and the block is locked in.

useCases.title: Triage what moved

faq.q: How does Husn track a dependency without me entering it?
faq.a: It reads how teams block, reference, and hand off across Jira, Slack, and docs, then tracks the state of each dependency from the live work rather than a typed-in record.

faq.q: What triggers an alert?
faq.a: A change in the other side's timing or intent, such as a deferred ticket, a moved date, or a thread that signals reprioritization, not just the arrival of a deadline.

faq.q: Does it change anything in our tools?
faq.a: No. Husn reads only. It never edits tickets, creates links, or writes anything back to your systems.

faq.q: How fast does the tracked state update?
faq.a: It reflects new activity as Husn reads it, so a paused ticket or a quiet handoff shows up as a change without anyone updating a tracker.

ctaHeadline: Track dependencies that warn you early.
ctaText: Connect your tools and Husn will track your live dependencies and alert the waiting team the moment the other side moves, in about fifteen minutes.

title: Release dependency management
metaDescription: Husn finds the dependencies a release rests on across Jira, Slack, and docs, then warns you when one of them slips, so launch day is not the first time you learn it.
heroHeadline: Know what your release is waiting on.
heroSubheadline: A release depends on more than its own backlog. Husn maps everything the launch rests on and tells you when any of it stops being on track.
primaryPain: A release looks ready right up until the moment a thing it quietly depended on fails to arrive. The release owner is accountable for work owned by other teams, but has no live view of whether those teams are actually going to deliver in time.
painBullets: Half the dependencies for a launch live on other teams' boards, where the release owner has no visibility and no warning.
Go or no-go meetings run on verbal assurances, and silence from a team gets read as readiness when it often means the opposite.
The dependency that sinks a release is usually a small enabling task that nobody flagged because it looked too minor to track.
whyHard: A release pulls in work from teams that do not share your timeline, so their reprioritization is invisible to you until it bites.
Readiness is assessed at a point in time, but the inputs keep moving right up to the freeze, and the early check goes stale.
The risky dependencies are often downstream of other dependencies, so a slip two steps removed reaches the release with no warning.
howHusnHelps: Husn assembles the full set of work a release depends on across Jira, Slack, and docs, including the enabling tasks owned by other teams.
It watches each of those dependencies and warns you when one moves, goes quiet, or gets deprioritized, well before the launch date.
It follows the chain, so a slip on a task the release depends on indirectly reaches you as a flagged risk, not a launch-day surprise.

faq.q: How does Husn know what a release depends on?

faq.q: Does it follow indirect dependencies?
faq.a: It does. Husn follows the chain, so a slip on something your release depends on through another team still reaches you as a flagged risk.

faq.q: Does Husn change our release plan or tickets?

ctaText: Connect your tools and Husn will map what your release depends on and flag the inputs that are slipping, in about fifteen minutes.

title: Blocker tracking software
metaDescription: Husn surfaces blockers across Jira, Slack, and docs as they form, tracks who owns the fix, and flags the ones that have stalled, without anyone logging them by hand.
heroEyebrow: For teams losing time to blockers
heroSubheadline: Most blockers are visible in the work days before they reach a standup. Husn surfaces them as they form and tracks them until someone actually clears them.
primaryPain: A blocker costs the most in the gap between when it starts and when it gets said out loud. Work quietly stalls, the person waiting assumes someone is handling it, and the blocker only becomes visible when a deadline forces it into a status update.
painBullets: Blockers are reported when someone remembers to raise them, so the quiet ones sit unmentioned for days while work stalls.
Once raised, a blocker rarely has a clear owner for the resolution, so it bounces between teams without moving.
Nobody tracks how long a blocker has been open, so the ones that have stalled the longest get the least attention.
whyHard: A blocker on one team is often caused by an unfinished task on another, and the two never appear in the same view.
Raising a blocker depends on the blocked person stopping to flag it, which is exactly what an overloaded person does not do.
Standups capture the blockers people choose to mention, not the ones forming quietly in stalled tickets and unanswered threads.
howHusnHelps: Husn surfaces blockers from the work itself across Jira, Slack, and docs, including stalled tickets and unanswered requests that nobody raised.
It connects each blocker to the work on the other side that would clear it, so the resolution has an owner rather than bouncing.
It tracks how long each blocker has been open and flags the ones that have stalled, so age becomes a signal instead of a blind spot.

faq.q: Can it tell me which blockers have stalled?
faq.a: Yes. Husn tracks how long each blocker has been open and flags the ones that have sat too long, so age becomes something you can act on.

faq.q: Does Husn change ticket status or assignees?
faq.a: No. It reads only. Husn never edits tickets, reassigns work, or writes anything back to your tools.

ctaHeadline: Catch the blocker while it still costs little.
ctaText: Connect your tools and Husn will surface active blockers, track their age, and point each one at an owner, in about fifteen minutes.

title: Critical path tracking
metaDescription: Husn keeps your critical path current from the live work across Jira, Slack, and docs, and warns you when something on it slips or a new item moves onto it.
heroHeadline: A critical path that stays true.
heroSubheadline: The critical path you drew at kickoff is not the one you are on now. Husn keeps it current from the work and tells you when the path itself shifts.
primaryPain: A critical path is usually mapped once, early, and then quietly diverges from reality as the work moves. The item you are watching most closely may no longer be the one that decides the date, and the item that now does may be one nobody is watching at all.
painBullets: The critical path is built at planning time and rarely rebuilt, so it reflects an early estimate rather than where the work actually is.
As tasks slip and re-sequence, a task that used to have slack becomes the constraint, and nobody notices the path has moved.
Keeping a critical path current by hand across many teams is constant work that gets abandoned within a few weeks of kickoff.
whyHardHeading: Why the path drifts from reality
whyHard: The path runs through work owned by several teams, so a slip on one board changes the constraint without anyone updating the plan.
Slack is what makes a task non-critical, and slack erodes silently, so the moment a task joins the critical path passes unobserved.
Recomputing the path means knowing the true state of every task on it, which no single person has across a large program.
howHusnHelps: Husn keeps the critical path current from the live state of the work across Jira, Slack, and docs, rather than from a one-time plan.
When a task on the path slips, or a task with shrinking slack moves onto it, Husn flags the change and what it does to your date.
It follows the path across team boundaries, so a slip several teams upstream reaches you as a warning about your delivery date.

title: Team handoff tracking
metaDescription: Husn tracks handoffs between teams across Jira, Slack, and docs, surfacing the ones that stalled, got dropped, or never landed, so work does not die in the gap.
heroEyebrow: For work that crosses many teams
heroHeadline: Track the work between the teams.
heroSubheadline: Work stalls most often in the gap between one team finishing and another picking up. Husn tracks those handoffs and surfaces the ones that did not land.
primaryPain: A handoff is the moment a piece of work changes hands, and it is exactly where ownership goes vague. The sending team believes they are done, the receiving team has not started, and the work sits in the gap with no one accountable until someone downstream notices it never arrived.
painBullets: A handoff is agreed in a meeting or a thread and then assumed complete, with no check that the receiving team actually picked it up.
Ownership is clear on each side and undefined in the middle, so a dropped handoff has no owner and no alarm.
The receiving team is often busy with other work, so a handoff can sit untouched for weeks before anyone realizes it stalled.
whyHard: The sending and receiving teams live on different boards, so neither system shows the handoff as a single piece of work with one status.
A handoff feels finished to the sender the moment they pass it on, which removes the very attention it needs to actually complete.
Across many teams there are dozens of handoffs in flight, and no one is responsible for watching the spaces between them.
howHusnHelps: Husn tracks handoffs from how teams pass work across Jira, Slack, and docs, following each one from where it leaves to where it should land.
It surfaces handoffs that stalled, got dropped, or were never acknowledged by the receiving team, before the gap turns into a delay.
It shows each handoff as one item with a status across both sides, so the space between teams stops being invisible.

title: Dependency risk management
metaDescription: Husn turns dependencies into managed risk, reading Jira, Slack, and docs to rank which dependencies are most likely to slip and warn the teams that would be hurt.
heroHeadline: Manage the risk a dependency carries.
heroSubheadline: Every dependency is a bet on another team. Husn tracks which of those bets is going wrong and tells the side that would be hurt, before it is.
primaryPain: A dependency is a risk wearing a friendly name. It looks like a line in a plan, but it is really an exposure to a team you do not control. Most organizations track the line and ignore the exposure, so the dependency that was always going to slip is treated the same as the one that never will, right up until it fails.
painBullets: Dependencies are recorded as facts, not as risks, so none of them carry a likelihood, an owner, or a contingency.
Every dependency looks equally safe in a list, which means attention spreads evenly instead of concentrating on the ones likely to slip.
The team carrying the exposure is the downstream one, but the signals that the bet is going wrong all live on the upstream team's board.
whyHard: Judging the risk in a dependency means knowing how the team you depend on is actually tracking, which is information you rarely have.
Risk is dynamic, so a dependency that was low risk last month can become the most likely point of failure without the register changing.
Second-order dependencies multiply the exposure, and the compound risk of a chain is invisible when each link is assessed alone.
howHusnHelps: Husn treats each dependency as a risk, reading Jira, Slack, and docs to judge how the team you depend on is actually tracking against the commitment.
It ranks dependencies by how likely they are to slip and how much depends on them, so attention concentrates where the exposure is highest.
When a dependency's risk rises, Husn warns the downstream team that carries the exposure, with the upstream signals that drove the change.

faq.a: It reads how the team you depend on is tracking across Jira, Slack, and docs, then judges the likelihood of a slip from the live signals rather than a static rating.

faq.q: How does it decide which dependencies matter most?
faq.a: Husn ranks them by how likely each is to slip and how much downstream work rests on it, so attention concentrates on the highest exposure.

faq.q: Can it handle risk in a chain of dependencies?
faq.a: Yes. Husn follows the chain and surfaces compound risk, so a fragile task several teams upstream shows up as a risk to everything that rests on it.

faq.q: Does Husn change anything in our tools?
faq.a: No. It reads only. Husn never edits tickets, sets risk fields, or writes anything back to your systems.

ctaHeadline: Treat every dependency as the risk it is.
ctaText: Connect your tools and Husn will rank your dependencies by risk and warn the exposed teams when the odds turn, in about fifteen minutes.

title: Roadmap dependency management
metaDescription: Husn maps the dependencies between roadmaps across Jira, Slack, and docs and warns you when one team's reprioritization breaks a commitment another roadmap was built on.
heroHeadline: When one roadmap moves, you know.
heroSubheadline: Roadmaps are planned in parallel but depend on each other in practice. Husn maps those links and warns you when a change on one breaks an assumption on another.
primaryPain: Roadmaps are built as if each team controls its own outcome, but one team's roadmap almost always rests on commitments inside another's. When a team reprioritizes its roadmap, it rarely traces which other roadmaps assumed the thing it just dropped, so the break only surfaces a quarter later when the dependent work cannot start.
painBullets: Each team plans its own roadmap in isolation, so the cross-roadmap dependencies that hold the plan together are never written down.
A reprioritization on one roadmap looks like a local decision, but it can quietly invalidate a commitment three other roadmaps were built on.
Roadmap dependencies are set at planning and never revisited, so by mid-quarter the plan rests on assumptions that are no longer true.
whyHardHeading: Why roadmaps break each other quietly
whyHard: Roadmaps live in different docs and boards at different altitudes, so no single view shows how one quarter's plan depends on another's.
The dependency is between a planned item and an assumption, and assumptions are exactly what teams forget to record or revisit.
Reprioritization is constant, and a change that is reasonable for one roadmap can be quietly destructive for another that depended on it.
howHusnHelps: Husn maps dependencies between roadmaps from how teams reference and commit to each other across Jira, Slack, and docs, including the unspoken assumptions.
When a team reprioritizes, Husn traces which other roadmaps assumed the thing that moved and warns the ones whose plan just changed.
It keeps the cross-roadmap picture current through the quarter, so a plan built on an assumption is flagged when the assumption breaks.

title: API dependency tracking
metaDescription: Husn tracks API and service dependencies between teams from Jira, Slack, and docs, flagging breaking changes and deprecations before they reach a consumer.
heroEyebrow: For teams that consume each other's APIs
heroHeadline: Track the APIs your teams rely on.
heroSubheadline: An API is a promise between teams, and promises change. Husn tracks which teams depend on which services and warns consumers when the contract is about to move.
primaryPain: When one team owns an API and several others build on it, a change to that API is a change to everyone downstream. The owning team makes the change for its own reasons, often without knowing who is still consuming the old contract, and the consumers find out when something breaks in their environment.
painBullets: The team that owns a service rarely has a current list of who is consuming it, so a deprecation goes out without reaching the people it affects.
Breaking changes are decided inside the owning team's tickets and threads, invisible to the consumers until the change ships.
API contracts are documented once and then drift, so the spec a consumer integrated against no longer matches what the service returns.
whyHard: Producer and consumer sit on separate boards, so a planned breaking change on one is invisible to the team that integrated against it.
The dependency is on a contract, and a contract can change in a code review or a thread long before any ticket says it is changing.
With many services depending on each other, a change to one API can cascade through services that depend on it indirectly.
howHusnHelps: Husn tracks which teams depend on which APIs and services from how they reference and integrate across Jira, Slack, and docs.
When an owning team plans a breaking change or deprecation, Husn flags it to the consumers still on the old contract, before it ships.
It follows service chains, so a change to one API reaches the teams that depend on it indirectly, not just the direct consumers.
